thread.title: Amazon's Increasing Profitability Means Its Fundamentals Are Changing - Amazon.com, Inc. AMZN)

author: Erich Reimer
title: Amazon's Increasing Profitability Means Its Fundamentals Are Changing - Amazon.com, Inc. AMZN)
text:
Amazon ( AMZN ) is a massive company that recently surpassed Google ( GOOGL ) as the second-largest U.S. company by public market capitalization. Despite earnings that are still a fraction of Google's, Amazon nonetheless has begun showing increasing profitability in recent months driven by its cloud services, advertising, and subscriptions segments.
As Amazon moves forward, it likely will begin to see a further contraction in its P/E multiple as it goes from a growth stage to operating on what its business model should be.
In the meantime Amazon's profitability likely will continue to grow and the transition will take time to fully take place, meaning that the downward price effect of a P/E multiple shrinkage will be countered by the still-present effects of how its currently valued on an optimistic growth basis.
What Does Amazon's Valuation Look Like Once It Has Settled Down? Back in April I wrote on how Amazon stock is experiencing a P/E ratio compression as its growth trajectory slows. The company's P/E ratio back then saw a decline from about 350 to around 177, based on its diluted EPS of $7.90 and then-price of around $1,400 per share.
Since then the company's P/E has expanded again steadily, although now to its previous heights. Currently Amazon's P/E valuation is now 217.211, which remains incredible as none of its peer tech behemoths have anywhere close to that kind of P/E ratio.
The only company that comes anywhere close is Netflix ( NFLX ), with its current P/E of 235.06 and $170.4 billion market cap based on EPS of $1.67.
Will there ever be a point where we could see Amazon move from its "growth" stage, as much as one can say for a $832.6 billion company, to a mature stage?
If Amazon ever does mature, its P/E ratio would likely contract to roughly 30-50, in line with other tech giants. While a 30-50 P/E ratio would be a growth-oriented ratio for most companies, given that secular trends are currently driving technology companies to inherently face innovative and growth demands it would likely be as mature as it could get at this point.
A 30 to 50 P/E would see either a shrinkage in price or an increase in EPS and thus earnings. A shrinkage on that level would reduce Amazon's price from its $1,715.97 to a mere $237 to $395 a share, or a drop of 86.2% to 76.9% respectively.
Thankfully that ultra-bearish future is unlikely, as I believe much of Amazon's earnings growth expectations are both here to stay for a while and likely will soon continue to materialize as it did in Q1 2018.
Were Amazon's earnings to increase instead of its price dropping, that means EPS would increase to $57.199 for a 30 P/E and $34.32 for a 50 P/E.
Based on 485 million common shares outstanding and 504 diluted shares outstanding, that would mean an increase in TTM net income to $28.828 billion to $17.297 billion, respectively.
In comparison, currently TTM net income is $3.938 billion, still the highest in Amazon history and a 52% year-on-year increase.
Based on that level of earnings, Amazon would really then look like a company in line with its peer tech giants that are raking in earnings at their behemoth market capitalizations. In 2017, Facebook ( FB ) brought in $15.934 billion in post-tax net income and Google ( GOOGL ) brought in $12.662 billion. Microsoft ( MSFT ) brought in TTM $ 12.225 billion, and Amazon is bigger than all of them except the profit-machine Apple ( AAPL ).
AMZN Market Cap data by YCharts
All of these companies experienced growth stages with high forward expectations before maturing, and undoubtedly someday Amazon will as well. The only questions are - how soon and in what ways?
Of course Amazon's price won't remain static as its business continue to mature, as its current valuation metrics driving it will continue to push its price up even as its P/E ratio begins to slowly shrink.
Can Amazon Get There? Amazon has multiple ways to increasing its profitability, as we saw in the most recent quarterly earnings. Though Amazon's public disclosures do not give a precise picture of the profitability of each segment, we do see that its overall operating margin has increased steadily over time.
In Q1 2018 it stood at a historic 3.8% for Amazon's total worldwide business. Amazon's North America segment's margin remained increasing but shaky, as it stood at 3.7%, down from the prior quarter's 4.5%. The international segment saw similar margins, as its -4.2% was better than the prior quarter's -5.1% or the -6.8% and -6.3% before that.
Amazon Web Services showed strong margins at still 25.7%, compared to the prior quarters' 26.5%, 25.5%, 22.3%, and 24.3%. This is as it has scaled up rapidly to $5.442 billion in revenue and $1.400 billion in operating income from year-on-year $3.661 billion in revenue and $890 million in operating income.
(Source: Amazon Q1 2018 Earnings )
Though margins for each particular product segment are unavailable, we nonetheless see substantial increases in Amazon's segments for high-margin business lines. These include its AWS cloud services, its subscription services (mainly Amazon Prime), and its "other," which is primarily its increasing online advertising program.
All of these businesses lines are inherently high-margin and high-growth, as compared to its retail business which has long shown weak, if even non-existent, margins.
Advertising in particular has the potential to boom Amazon's earnings significantly, as companies like Google and Facebook have shown it is a high-margin business. Amazon is already showing consistent year-on-year gains there, with its most recent quarter posting a 139% increase.
In short, can Amazon eventually reach $20 billion to $30 billion, or more, from its current $3.938 billion in net income to justify its current price? Undoubtedly yes. The expected growth in cloud, advertising, subscriptions, and other services are profitable operationally and only expected to scale up.
As for Amazon's growth prospects itself in terms of increasing its valuation? There are still likely moderate gains to be expected, but I believe its business is also maturing as it now begins to show its profitability. It likely will continue to grow as its former valuation methods continue to counter its shrinking growth multiple, but with restrained growth compared to its 77.97% gain this past year or 305% gain the past 3 years.
AMZN data by YCharts
Conclusion Amazon is a gigantic company that brings in immense revenue and now increasingly earnings as well. Now that it is beginning to show profits, that means it is moving forward in its business life cycle and likely will begin to see a contraction in P/E that pushes against its expected earnings growth.
However for Amazon this doesn't mean that it won't stop rallying in valuation, as the transition from its growth-stage to its regular business operations stage will take time. In the meantime, Amazon likely will continue to see some growth still as its very high P/E continues to hold up to some degree with its increasing earnings.
Amazon was laughed at for years because it could not post profits or earnings. It now seemingly has finally found ways to do so through a combination of cloud services, subscriptions, and advertising, with other potential operations down the line as well. Amazon has rewarded those investors that have believed in it, and it may continue to do so to some, but a smaller, degree.
